Learn more | Search MSDN Search all blogs Search this blog Sign in Midnight Musings of a Technical TAM Midnight Musings of a Technical TAM Providing technical information and guidance for Microsoft customers Group Policy Basics \xe2\x80\x93 Part 1: Understanding the Structure of a Group Policy Object \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 \xe2\x98 srachuiFebruary 13, 201229 Share 0 0 As a Windows administrator, you almost certainly have used Group Policies to control the settings deployed to the clients of your Active Directory infrastructure.\xc2 But with Group Policies getting such heavy use, not as many administrators fully understand how Group Policy Objects (GPOs) are structured.\xc2 In this post, I will discuss the structure of GPOs in order to help bring greater understanding to this topic.\xc2 When you're troubleshooting Group Policies in your environment, it's helpful to understand how they're structured, and hopefully this post will clear up a bit of that mystery. Group Policy Objects are actually composed of two parts, the Group Policy Container (GPC)\xc2 which\xc2 exists in Active Directory and the Group Policy Template (GPT) where the actual content of your GPOs resides.\xc2 A third component, known as Client-Side Extensions (CSEs) can be found on client devices and are necessary for them to properly process the Group Policies assigned to them. Before we go through these individual pieces, take a look at how GPOs show up when viewed through the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC). In the early days of Active Directory, the only real way to get to a GPO is to open the location where it was linked (a domain, organizational unit, or site).\xc2 This made it appear that the GPOs existed at those place in the directory when they were actually only linked to those locations so that their settings would apply to the specified objects they contained (such as the computer objects within a particular OU).\xc2 With the GPMC, it's much clearer to see that GPOs do not reside at these different points of the directory but instead exist separately and are only linked to these different levels. To see an example of where a GPO is linked, you can check the Scope tab of your selected GPO within the GPMC, as shown below. You can see from this picture that the GPO I created named Event Log Size is linked to the Workstations OU within the W2K8Forest domain.\xc2 You can further see that the link is enabled (meaning the policy will apply), but it is not enforced (meaning that the policy can be blocked if the administrator of the Workstations OU wishes to prevent the policy applying). But even the GPMC's view of where GPOs reside is a bit misleading as there really is no Group Policy Object container in Active Directory.\xc2 Instead, the actual structure of the GPO is laid out as follows. Group Policy Container (GPC) The first piece of the GPO, while not within a container called Group Plicy Objects,\xc2 is still found within Active Directory.\xc2 In order to see it, there are several options.\xc2 The most common is to use Active Directory Users and Computers.\xc2 If you choose this tool, you'll need to take the following steps to see the appropriate folder: Open Active Directory Users and Computers (you can do this by typing DSA.MSC at Start/Run) Select View from the menu bar and ensure Advanced Features is selected (if not, select it) Expand the System\xc2 container and navigate to the Policies container If you don't enable Advanced Features, you won't see the System container.\xc2 But after this is enabled, you should have a screen similar to the one below: Notice that there are two containers, each with a string of numbers.\xc2 Each of these represents a different GPO (the string of numbers is the Globally Unique Identifier, or GUID, of each GPO).\xc2 Within each of these containers you'll see a Machine and User container.\xc2 These contain specific information related to the User and Machine nodes of the GPO itself (as you might expect, the Machine node refers to computer settings and the User node refers to user settings). Another tool that you can use to view these folders is LDP.\xc2 To use LDP to see these folders, take the following steps: Start LDP by typing LDP.EXE at Start/Run Select Connections from the menu bar and select Connect... to connect to the Domain Controller of your choice.\xc2 Select OK enter the fully qualified domain name of the Domain Controller enter port 389 since you're doing an LDAP query Select Connections again and choose Bind... Make sure you are binding to the directory with an account that has sufficient permissions to do an LDAP query Select\xc2 View and choose Tree.\xc2 Enter the distinguished name of your domain (for example: dc=W2K8Forest,dc=com).\xc2 Select OK In the left-hand column, expand the directory tree and navigate to Policies under the System container There is one big difference when using LDP, which becomes immediately obvious after selecting one of the GPO nodes.\xc2 When you double-click it, you will suddenly see a great deal of information in the right-hand pane.\xc2 This is the critical directory information that client machines use when processing GPOs.\xc2 These settings allow clients to understand where the content of the policy is, which Client-Side Extensions will be needed to process the GPO content, etc. Here is a screenshot of what you'll see within the LDP window: Looking at the details of our selected GPO, there are several attributes which are of special interest to us: displayName: This attribute is the human-friendly name of your GPO gPCFileSysPath: This attribute points clients to the location where the GPO content can be found.\xc2 Collectively, this is known as the Group Policy Template, which is housed in a share known as SYSVOL gPCMachineExtensionNames: Here is the list of Client-Side Extensions (CSEs)\xc2 that will be needed by the client in order to process all of the machine-side\xc2 settings configured for this GPO gPCUserExtensionNames: This attribute contains the list of CSEs that will be needed to process the user-side settings.\xc2 As there are no user-side settings configured in this GPO, the attribute is not populated (and thus not displayed) Another important attribute is gPLink and while it's not found as part of the GPO itself, you can find this attribute everywhere that the GPO is linked.\xc2 This allows objects within these other containers to know that there is a GPO it needs to process.\xc2 In the screenshot below, you can see that the gPLink attribute points to a single GPO found within the policies container of the system partition: So now we've seen the Active Directory portion of the Group Policy object.\xc2 It contains settings so that the client can learn which GPOs it must process, which tools it will need to process them, and how to locate the GPO contents in order to process.\xc2 Now that we've seen the first part, let's take a look at how and where\xc2 the GPO content itself is stored. Group Policy Template (GPT) The Group Policy Template is where the meat of the GPO resides.\xc2 By way of comparison, think of how Active Directory represents a computer object.\xc2 It lists all the relevant attributes of the computer, but the object in Active Directory is not the computer itself.\xc2 In a similar way, the portion of the GPO in Active Directory merely represents the attributes relevant to the GPO content.\xc2 The content itself is known as the Group Policy Template, or GPT, and it resides in a share known as SYSVOL.\xc2 This share, like the portion of the GPO stored in Active Directory, is replicated to\xc2 every DC in the domain.\xc2 This way, when a client queries for the GPOs it needs to process, it can locate the contents of those GPOs on the same (in most cases) DC where it's conducting the query. NOTE: The only exception to this rule is cross-domain GPOs where a GPO is defined in another domain, but is linked in such a way that clients from neighboring domains need to apply them (a Site-level GPO is an example, since Active Directory Sites can span multiple domains).\xc2 In the case of a cross-domain GPO, the client will need to pull content from a DC in the neighboring domain which can be a very slow process.\xc2 For this reason, cross-domain GPOs are not generally recommended. To see the content of your GPOs, you'll want to look at the SYSVOL share on one of your DCs.\xc2 You can find the SYSVOL share by navigating to %windir%/sysvol/sysvol (yes, there is a shared SYSVOL folder within a parent SYSVOL folder).\xc2 The actual sysvol share is set to \\\\<servername>\\sysvol\xc2 Within this folder, you will see the same list of GPOs that appear within Active Directory's System/Policies container.\xc2 These folders are where the actual settings of your GPO are contained.\xc2 Depending on the number of settings you've put in place, there will be more or less present in each folder.\xc2 Regardless, you are guaranteed to have at least the following folders/files within each of your GPOs: %windir% sysvol sysvol (shared as \\\\servername\\sysvol) <domain name> Policies scripts Within the policies folder, you'll find the various GPOs and their configured settings.\xc2 Again, the following folders/files are guaranteed to be present for every GPO in your domain: Policies <GPO GUID> Machine (folder containing the computer-side settings of the GPO) User (folder containing the user-side settings of the GPO) GPT.INI (file containing the GPO's configuration settings) Depending on what you've configured, the Machine and User folders may or may not contain additional content.\xc2 As an illustration, lets take a look at the contents of a GPO I've configured to set the various Event Logs on my clients to their maximum size.\xc2 First, here is the Group Policy Management Editor showing the settings I've configured.\xc2 This is the tool you'll be working with when you configure the settings for your own environment. If you need to know how to launch this tool, you do so from within the Group Policy Management Console by right-clicking your GPO and selecting Edit... as shown below. So now that you understand how to make these changes, what does the GPT look like once you've made them?\xc2 Below is a series of screenshots to answer that question. First, here is the file structure of the GPT, showing the GPO I've edited with its top level folders visible in the right-hand pane You'll notice the file called GPT (it's actually GPT.INI, though the screenshot hides the file extension).\xc2 This file contains the configuration settings for this GPO, which includes its current version number (which is updated every time a change to the GPO is made) and the default GPO display\xc2 name (which is the same for every GPO you create, so don't worry that it's not the name you gave it in the GPMC).\xc2 Here is how that file looks (NOTE: You can open GPT.INI with Notepad, but make sure you don't accidentally save it as a .txt file or it will impact your GPOs ability to do its job) To see the actual settings we've configured for this GPO, we need to expand the Machine folder (because this is a computer-side setting), which reveals the following: You'll notice that there is a folder called SecEdit, which contains the security-specific settings of this GPO.\xc2 The file within the SecEdit folder is GptTmpl.inf.\xc2 It's this file that contains the specific information that your client needs to configure its settings.\xc2 Because we've configured this GPO so that its Event Logs are set at the maximum size, we would expect that this file would contain information directing the client to make this change.\xc2 By opening the file we can see that its contents do exactly as we would expect, as shown below\xc2 (NOTE: you can edit it with Notepad, but make sure you don't accidentally save it [or GPT.INI]\xc2 as a .txt file after looking at it!). We can see from this picture that GptTmpl.inf has clear instructions for our client machine to set its Application, Security and System Event Logs to their maximum size. As I said earlier, there can be numerous different settings in the GPT file structure depending on how you've configured your GPO.\xc2 Other possible folders and files that might appear include: Scripts folder\xc2 - This folder can contain information on which scripts to run, or may include the scripts themselves.\xc2 The possible types of scripts include: Startup/Shutdown: applies to Computers Logon/Logoff: applies to Users Applications folder\xc2 - if you've published or advertised software through a GPO, this folder will contain an advertisement file (.aas file extension) notifying clients of the software being made available Adm folder - Older GPO versions had Administrative Templates stored within the GPT on each Domain Controller.\xc2 These templates were actually copied from client machines into the SYSVOL share of the Domain Controller.\xc2 Starting with Vista, GPOs no longer do this (though if you edit a GPO with an\xc2 pre-Vista OS, it will still\xc2 behave this way).\xc2 GPOs now\xc2 leverage ADMX files that are stored in a Central Store on client machines\xc2 (typically c:\\windows\\policydefinitions) instead of the GPT.\xc2 But given that many older devices are still out there, you may see this folder in your GPT. Documents and Settings folder\xc2 - this folder contains any Folder Redirectoin settings configured by the GPO. IEAK folder - this user-side\xc2 folder contains settings related to Internet Explorer Maintenance. Registry.pol - this file contains the registry settings the GPO has been configured to apply.\xc2 This file also contains\xc2 any Software Restriction Policy settings that have been configured. In part 2 of this series, we'll look at details of GPO processing, with an emphasis on Client-Side Extensions (CSEs).\xc2 We'll also discuss how GPOs are replicated, and how a client knows it's getting the latest version of its GPO (including knowing whether the GPC and GPC are synchronized with each other). \xc2 Tags active directory gpc gpo gpt gpt.ini group policy policies Comments (29) Anonymous says: September 17, 2019 at 10:51 pm Good note, thanks for sharing \xf0\x9f\x99\x82 Sajoor says: September 17, 2019 at 10:51 pm No words\xe2\x80\xa6this is an excellent article! Group Policy Objects are actually composed of two parts, the Group Policy Container (GPC)\xc2 which\xc2 exists in Active Directory and the Group Policy Template (GPT) where the actual content of your GPOs resides.\xc2 A third component, known as Client-Side Extensions (CSEs) can be found on client devices and are necessary for them to properly process the Group Policies assigned to them.
Before we go through these individual pieces, take a look at how GPOs show up when viewed through the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC).
To see an example of where a GPO is linked, you can check the Scope tab of your selected GPO within the GPMC, as shown below.

You can see from this picture that the GPO I created named Event Log Size is linked to the Workstations OU within the W2K8Forest domain.\xc2 You can further see that the link is enabled (meaning the policy will apply), but it is not enforced (meaning that the policy can be blocked if the administrator of the Workstations OU wishes to prevent the policy applying).

But even the GPMC's view of where GPOs reside is a bit misleading as there really is no Group Policy Object container in Active Directory.\xc2 Instead, the actual structure of the GPO is laid out as follows.

Another tool that you can use to view these folders is LDP.\xc2 To use LDP to see these folders, take the following steps: Start LDP by typing LDP.EXE at Start/Run Select Connections from the menu bar and select Connect... to connect to the Domain Controller of your choice.\xc2 Select OK enter the fully qualified domain name of the Domain Controller enter port 389 since you're doing an LDAP query Select Connections again and choose Bind...

NOTE: The only exception to this rule is cross-domain GPOs where a GPO is defined in another domain, but is linked in such a way that clients from neighboring domains need to apply them (a Site-level GPO is an example, since Active Directory Sites can span multiple domains).\xc2 In the case of a cross-domain GPO, the client will need to pull content from a DC in the neighboring domain which can be a very slow process.\xc2 For this reason, cross-domain GPOs are not generally recommended.
If you need to know how to launch this tool, you do so from within the Group Policy Management Console by right-clicking your GPO and selecting Edit... as shown below.
Documents and Settings folder\xc2 - this folder contains any Folder Redirectoin settings configured by the GPO.
IEAK folder - this user-side\xc2 folder contains settings related to Internet Explorer Maintenance.
Registry.pol - this file contains the registry settings the GPO has been configured to apply.\xc2 This file also contains\xc2 any Software Restriction Policy settings that have been configured.
